children: post-IPO slide is sharpening questions about how the AI company will finance its $900B spending commitments, with bond investors expecting its debt to receive a junk rating, The Wall Street Journal reported.
The company's shares fell 6.54% on Tuesday to $81.91, slipping below their $83 IPO price after opening at $111.50 on November 19. The stock had already dropped 8.5% on Friday.
Anthropic's spending commitments cover the computing power needed for its AI models. Its IPO and a concurrent private placement raised more than $100B last week, but the company remains unprofitable.
The WSJ reported that the company also had about $96B in cash, which analysts say, together with the offering proceeds, could fund its spending commitments for a year or more.

Several large bond-fund managers expect rating firms to place Anthropic in the BB range, a notch, or two short of investment grade. That would make it by far the most valuable U.S. company with a high-yield credit rating, ahead of Hilton Worldwide, whose market value is about $80B, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
An investment-grade rating would give Anthropic access to the $8.6T high-grade corporate bond market. It could also ease pressure on chipmakers Nvidia
, which have guaranteed tens of billions of dollars in loans to buyers of their chips, which are then rented to AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI.
Fund managers said Anthropic is unlikely to issue many unsecured bonds because the junk-bond market is relatively small, at $1.7T, and carries high borrowing costs.
Roughly half of Anthropic's spending commitments do not begin until 2030, and without an investment-grade rating by then, the company could struggle to pay its bills, the WSJ reported.
"They have about three years of runway to get investors particularly comfortable with the credit story," Neil Sun, a bond-fund manager at RBC Global Asset Management, told WSJ.

title: Anthropic faces junk-debt doubts as AI borrowing surges
